title: Preview of Calculus
summary: This section bridges the gap between static pre-calculus mathematics and the dynamic nature of calculus by addressing two fundamental problems: determining the slope of a tangent line to a curve and calculating the instantaneous velocity of a moving object. Both problems are solved using the same limiting process, where approximations—such as the slopes of secant lines or average velocities over shrinking time intervals—converge to a single, precise value. This concept of the "limit" serves as the foundation for the entire course, establishing the mathematical tools necessary to analyze instantaneous rates of change.

title: Functions and Limits
summary: This chapter formalizes the concept of the limit, moving from intuitive approximations to rigorous mathematical definitions including the precise Epsilon-Delta definition. It provides the algebraic rules (Limit Laws) necessary to calculate limits without graphing, methods for handling indeterminate forms, and defines continuity to describe functions without breaks or holes. These concepts culminate in the Intermediate Value Theorem, a powerful tool used to prove the existence of roots and solutions within specific intervals, setting the stage for the definition of the derivative.

The Precise Definition of a Limit

title: Derivatives
summary: This chapter turns the limiting process of the previous chapter into a machine: the derivative. Starting from rates of change and the derivative as a function in its own right, it builds the full computational toolkit (the power, product, quotient and chain rules, derivatives of trigonometric functions, and implicit differentiation) before returning to the real world with rates of change in science and society and the idea of linear approximation, where a curve is deliberately replaced by its own tangent line.

pages.title: Rates of Change in Science and Society

title: Applications of Differentiation
summary: Here the derivative stops being a formula and starts being an instrument. The Extreme Value Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem provide the theory; increasing-decreasing behavior, concavity, and asymptotes provide the vocabulary for reading the shape of any graph. The chapter culminates in systematic curve sketching, optimization problems that turn geometry and physics into calculus, Newton's method for hunting roots numerically, and a first look at antiderivatives, the doorway into integration.

pages.title: Derivatives & The Shape of a Graph

title: Integrals
summary: This chapter solves the area and distance problems posed at the very start of the course. Riemann sums chop a region into thin rectangles, and their limit defines the definite integral: a single number recording accumulated change. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus then reveals the astonishing fact that accumulation and differentiation undo one another, collapsing area computations into antiderivative lookups. The chapter closes with the substitution rule, the chain rule run backward, and the symmetry shortcuts it explains.

pages.title: Indefinite Integrals and the Net Change Theorem

title: Applications of Integration
summary: One idea powers this whole chapter: slice the object, understand one slice, and let the integral add the slices back up. Vertical and horizontal slices measure areas between curves; slices revolved around an axis become disks, washers, and cylindrical shells that measure volume; slices of a rope or a tank of water measure the work done against gravity; and dividing accumulated area by the width of the interval defines the average value of a function.

title: Inverse Functions
summary: Reflection across the line y = x generates an entire zoo of new functions. The natural logarithm is born from the area under 1/t, its inverse is the exponential function, and together they explain every other base, growth and decay processes, and logarithmic differentiation. Restricting the trigonometric functions yields their inverses, exponentials in disguise yield the hyperbolic functions, and the chapter ends with l'Hospital's Rule, the definitive tool for the indeterminate forms these functions constantly produce.

title: Techniques of Integration
summary: Differentiation is mechanical; integration is an art of recognition. This chapter assembles the working integrator's toolbox: integration by parts for products, identity games for trigonometric powers, trigonometric substitution for roots of quadratics, partial fractions for rational functions, and an overall strategy for choosing among them. It then confronts integrals that resist exact methods, with tables, technology, and the Trapezoidal and Simpson's Rules, and finishes with improper integrals, where areas over infinite regions are tamed by limits, p-tests, and comparison.
